To fix (2)

To fix Power Analysis Check

What we found

We detected 1 potential power analysis.

Show details

We used the LLM model ‘vllm/DeepSeek-V41-Flash-1017-FP8’ to check the contents of 1 paragraph that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses.

Some essential information could not be detected: software

power_type statistical_test sample_size alpha_level power effect_size effect_size_metric software
apriori paired t-test 198 0.05 0.8 0.2 Cohen’s d NA
text
Samples with balanced quotas for age (five categories: 20% 18-29 years, 20% 30-39 years, 20% 40-49 years, 20% 50-59 years, 20% 60 years and older) and gender (two categories: 50% male, 50% female) were collected by the market research company Bilendi & respondi with the use of online questionnaires programmed in Qualtrics ten days before and three weeks after the referendum on June 18, 2023. Sample size was determined based on a power analysis for a different, non-overlapping paper (see pre-registration and Cologna et al., 2024). We also considered expected attrition and failure rates for the attention checks (two in the pre-referendum and one in the post-referendum survey). A power analysis for using a paired-samples t-test indicated that a total sample size of approximately 198 participants would be required to detect a small effect size (Cohen’s d = 0.2) with 80% power at a 5% significance level (two-tailed). Our sample of 827 participants clearly exceeds this number.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 2 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Text Sentence
p = .491 Among participants who completed both surveys before and after the referendum, we see that others’ perceptions of advocacy thus remains unchanged among the same participants before (N = 827, M = 3.34, SD = 0.98) and after (N = 827, M = 3.31, SD = 0.93) the referendum (95% CI of mean difference [-0.09, 0.04], t(826) = -0.69, d = -.02, p = .491; Figure 2a-2b, see also Table S4), as did the discrepancy between perceived advocacy support and actual advocacy support pre and post referendum (t(826) = 1.012, d = .04, p = .312).
p = .312 Among participants who completed both surveys before and after the referendum, we see that others’ perceptions of advocacy thus remains unchanged among the same participants before (N = 827, M = 3.34, SD = 0.98) and after (N = 827, M = 3.31, SD = 0.93) the referendum (95% CI of mean difference [-0.09, 0.04], t(826) = -0.69, d = -.02, p = .491; Figure 2a-2b, see also Table S4), as did the discrepancy between perceived advocacy support and actual advocacy support pre and post referendum (t(826) = 1.012, d = .04, p = .312).

For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see:

Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742.

Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167.

For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see Improving Your Statistical Inferences.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. setwd() calls were found in 1 code file.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). install.packages() calls were found in 2 code files.

Careless Responding

926 distinct respondents were flagged for straightlining: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is one row per person, and the Longest run column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, 665 were flagged only by short-scale straightlining (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.

These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

Showing the first 500 of 926 rows.

What this does not cover. Only 7 of 8 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

All detected t-tests and F-tests had an effect size reported in the same sentence.

Fine

Reproducibility Check

  • We assessed AND ran 2 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
  • 2 of 2 scripts ran without error when executed.
  • 15 installable dependencies detected.
  • 1489 statistics stored from the extracted output; 5 of 22 reported tests matched (22.7%).

See the section Reproducibility Check below for the details.

Reproducibility Check

We ran the paper’s 2 R scripts in the order they depend on each other, each in an isolated container, for at most 5 minutes per script.

2 of 2 scripts ran to the end.

Script Result What happened
ORIGINAL_do-not-use_CPL_advocacy_06DEC24.R Ran to the end
CORRECTED_CPL_advocacy_24JUN25_newIDs.R Ran to the end

Other problems in the files

  • ORIGINAL_do-not-use_CPL_advocacy_06DEC24.R calls setwd(), which ties the script to a folder on the author’s computer. We replaced the call with one that does nothing so the script could run; it should be removed from the script.

Comparison with the paper

Of the 22 statistical tests reported in the paper, 5 were found in the output of the code.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 2 R code files.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), source() calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

Order File Runs after Basis
1 ORIGINAL_do-not-use_CPL_advocacy_06DEC24.R — numeric
2 CORRECTED_CPL_advocacy_24JUN25_newIDs.R — numeric

File paths

8 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited. We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: data_CPLadvocacy-pre-vote_RESAMPLE.csv to ../Datasets/ORIGINAL datasets_do-not-use/data_CPLadvocacy-pre-vote_RESAMPLE.csv (in ORIGINAL_do-not-use_CPL_advocacy_06DEC24.R); data_CPLadvocacy-pre-vote_NEW.csv to ../Datasets/ORIGINAL datasets_do-not-use/data_CPLadvocacy-pre-vote_NEW.csv (in ORIGINAL_do-not-use_CPL_advocacy_06DEC24.R); data_CPLadvocacy-post-vote_CONTROL.csv to ../Datasets/ORIGINAL datasets_do-not-use/data_CPLadvocacy-post-vote_CONTROL.csv (in ORIGINAL_do-not-use_CPL_advocacy_06DEC24.R); data_CPLadvocacy-post-vote_TREATMENT.csv to ../Datasets/ORIGINAL datasets_do-not-use/data_CPLadvocacy-post-vote_TREATMENT.csv (in ORIGINAL_do-not-use_CPL_advocacy_06DEC24.R); data_CPLadvocacy-pre-vote_RESAMPLE_corrected.xlsx to ../Datasets/CORRECTED datasets/data_CPLadvocacy-pre-vote_RESAMPLE_corrected.xlsx (in CORRECTED_CPL_advocacy_24JUN25_newIDs.R); data_CPLadvocacy-pre-vote_NEW_corrected.xlsx to ../Datasets/CORRECTED datasets/data_CPLadvocacy-pre-vote_NEW_corrected.xlsx (in CORRECTED_CPL_advocacy_24JUN25_newIDs.R); data_CPLadvocacy-post-vote_CONTROL_corrected.xlsx to ../Datasets/CORRECTED datasets/data_CPLadvocacy-post-vote_CONTROL_corrected.xlsx (in CORRECTED_CPL_advocacy_24JUN25_newIDs.R); data_CPLadvocacy-post-vote_TREATMENT_corrected.xlsx to ../Datasets/CORRECTED datasets/data_CPLadvocacy-post-vote_TREATMENT_corrected.xlsx (in CORRECTED_CPL_advocacy_24JUN25_newIDs.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 2 scripts: 2 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

File Outcome Detail Time (s)
ORIGINAL_do-not-use_CPL_advocacy_06DEC24.R ran_ok 11.6
CORRECTED_CPL_advocacy_24JUN25_newIDs.R ran_ok 12.7

setwd() in the code

1 script calls setwd(). This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after ignoring a setwd() that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed.

Reproducible after removing setwd(): ORIGINAL_do-not-use_CPL_advocacy_06DEC24.R.

File setwd() removed Path(s) it set
ORIGINAL_do-not-use_CPL_advocacy_06DEC24.R 1 (non-literal)

Calls that install packages in the code

28 calls to install.packages(), groundhog, checkpoint, renv, pacman and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: groundhog.library() and p_load() by library(), the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.

Reported vs. reproduced

22 statistical tests reported in the manuscript text were checked against the extracted analysis output: 5 matched (3 fully, 2 partially) — 22.7% found.

Some reported values were only found alongside OTHER components after being separated from their own originally-reported neighbours (e.g. a mean split from its own confidence interval). The “Plausible” column marks whether that split is well-supported: TRUE when the pieces still trace back to the same underlying variable (via the output’s own row labels), FALSE when no such link was found — a FALSE match is not necessarily wrong, but is worth checking against its own Source file/Analysis columns before treating it as confirmed.

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

For a separate study (Cologna et al., 2024), participants were randomly assigned to a control or treatment condition in the pre-referendum study, but due to an error from the market research company, some participants were not reassigned to the same experimental condition post-referendum.

Finally, panel attrition checks, which examined whether baseline demographic, attitudinal and experimental variables predicted whether participants completed the post-referendum survey, showed that older participants and participants in the control (vs. treatment) condition used in the other study were more likely to remain in the study (see Table S2).

After answering questions on their own and others’ climate change concern and others’ support for scientists’ advocacy in the pre-referendum survey, participants were randomly assigned to a control or a treatment condition (note that assignment to a treatment or control condition was for a different study).

In the post-referendum survey, participants were informed about the voting outcome in their canton of residence.

Participants were then asked about their own and others’ concern about climate change and advocacy support.

We recruited a large sample that is representative of the Swiss population in terms of age, gender, and tertiary education, but may not be exactly representative for income and political orientation (see Table S1).

All subjects gave informed consent.

Ethics approval statement:

Therefore, the Harvard University Area Committee on the Use of Human Subjects determined that no further ethics approval was needed for this study.

id title template
fd9vs How collective policy advocacy affects trust in scientists: A case study of the Swiss Climate Protection Law OSF Preregistration

Meta-scientific research has shown that deviations from preregistrations are often not reported or checked, and that the most common deviations concern the sample size. We recommend manually checking the full preregistration at the link above, and have provided the preregistered sample size.

id sample_size
fd9vs In Study 1 (Time 2 - pre-voting), we will invite n = 1,018 participants who participated in our survey in February 2023 (Time 1) to complete our online survey. According to the market research company Bilendi & Respondi, we can expect a recall rate of about 60%, i.e., about n = 600. We will additionally recruit n = 1,050 for a total sample of n = 1,650 at Time 2.

In Study 2 (Time 3 - post-voting), we will invite all participants that completed Study 1 (Time 2- pre-voting). With a recall rate of about 60% (and excluding participants that failed our attention checks at Time 2), we expect to be able to recruit n = 891 at Time 3.

research_questions RQ1a: What is the level of support (voting intentions) for the CPL at T2?

RQ1b: Which variables influence support (voting intentions) for the CPL at T2?
H1b: Support for the CPL at T2 is associated with the following variables: (1) trust in scientists at T1, (2) party preference (SVP vs other), (3) political orientation, (4) climate change concern, (5) condition (treatment vs. control), (6) gender, (7) being a father to a daughter, (8) language region, (9) urban/rural, (10) age, (11) income

RQ2a: Is there a statistically significant difference in trust in scientists between the control group and treatment group at T2?
H2a: Trust in scientists will be significantly higher in the treatment group than in the control group at T2.

RQ2b: Do political orientation and party preference (SVP vs. others) moderate the effect of treatment vs. control on trust in scientists at T2?
H2b: We hypothesize a negative effect of treatment vs. control on trust in scientists among SVP supporters and more right-leaning individuals at T2.

RQ2c: Is there a statistically significant difference in the normative perceptions of scientists in policymaking between the control group and treatment group at T2?
H2c: Normative perceptions of scientists in policymaking will be significantly higher in the treatment group than in the control group at T2.

RQ2d: Do political orientation and party preference (SVP vs. others) moderate the effect of treatment vs. control on normative perceptions of scientists in policymaking at T2?
H2d: We hypothesize a negative effect of treatment vs. control on normative perceptions of scientists in policymaking among SVP supporters and more right-leaning individuals at T2.

RQ2e: Is there a statistically significant difference in the voting intentions between the control group and treatment group at T2?
H2e: Voting intentions will be significantly higher in the treatment group than in the control group at T2.

RQ2f: Do political orientation and party preference (SVP vs. others) moderate the effect of treatment vs. control on voting intentions at T2?
H2f: We hypothesize a negative effect of treatment vs. control on voting intentions among SVP supporters and more right-leaning individuals at T2.


RQ3a: Is there a statistically significant difference in trust in scientists between the control group and treatment group at T3?
H3a: Trust in scientists will be significantly higher in the treatment group than in the control group at T3.

RQ3b: Does voting behavior (yes vs. no) moderate the effect of treatment vs. control on trust in scientists at T3?
H3b: We hypothesize a negative effect of treatment vs. control on trust in scientists for participants who voted against the CPL at T3.

RQ3c: Is there a statistically significant difference in normative perceptions of scientists in policymaking between the control group and treatment group at T3?
H3c: Normative perceptions of scientists in policymaking will be significantly higher in the treatment group than in the control group at T3.

RQ3d: Does voting behavior (yes vs. no) moderate the effect of treatment vs. control on normative perceptions of scientists in policymaking at T3?
H3d: We hypothesize a negative effect of treatment vs. control on normative perceptions of scientists in policymaking for participants who voted against the CPL at T3.


RQ4: Does observing the voting outcome influence a) normative perceptions, b) trust in science, c) support for climate change policies and d) beliefs about the views of other people in Switzerland at T3? (Treatment: showing each participant the voting result for their canton/voting district)
H4: Observing a YES vote increases a) normative perceptions, b) trust in science, c) support for climate change policies and d) beliefs about other people’s support for the CPL and for scientists advocacy, and about their concern about climate change


RQ5a: What is participants’ perceived level of support for the CPL among other people in Switzerland at T2?
H5a: The perceived level of support for the CPL among other people in Switzerland will be underestimated.

RQ5b: What is participants’ perceived level of concern about climate change among other people in Switzerland at T2?
H5b: The perceived level of concern about climate change among other people in Switzerland will be underestimated.

RQ5c: What is participants’ perceived level of support for scientists’ climate policy advocacy among other people in Switzerland at T2?
H5c: The perceived level of support for scientists’ climate policy advocacy among other people in Switzerland will be underestimated.
study_type Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
blinding For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned.
q5 No
study_design_overview Our study is a longitudinal online survey in Switzerland with an experiment embedded in the survey. In February 2023, data from n = 1,018 Swiss participants was collected (Time 1). In June 2023, participants who completed the survey in Time 1 will be invited to complete a survey with an embedded experiment in which participants will be randomly assigned to one of two conditions: control vs. treatment (Time 2). We will additionally recruit more participants who will also randomly be assigned to one of the two conditions to ensure adequate sample size/statistical power given the anticipated attrition between waves. All participants who completed the survey at Time 2 will also be invited to participate in a third online study with an embedded experiment in June 2023 (Time 3), in which participants will be assigned to the same condition (control vs. treatment) as in Time 2.
randomization Participants will randomly be assigned to either a control or a treatment condition at Time 2 and reassigned to the same condition at Time 3.
existing_data Registration prior to creation of data
existing_data_explanation For some analyses, we will use data collected at Time 1 (before any manipulation occurred).
data_collection_procedures We will collect data in two online surveys with experiments embedded in Switzerland in June 2023. The first survey will be conducted before 18 June 2023 and the second after 18 June 2023.

Respondents will be recruited from an online panel provided by the market research company Bilendi & Respondi. Respondents will receive vouchers/credit points for completing the full survey, which they can redeem and/or transfer into money.

In order to be able to complete the survey, respondents must:
- Agree with the terms and conditions of the consent form
- Be at least 18 years old
- Pass a first attention check, which asks them to write “213” in a text box
- Pass a second attention check, which asks them to indicate a) How many signatures are needed to launch a popular initiative in the control group; b) How many scientists signed a statement in support of the climate protection law in the treatment group.
- At T3, pass one attention check, which asks them to write “600” in a text box.
sample_size In Study 1 (Time 2 - pre-voting), we will invite n = 1,018 participants who participated in our survey in February 2023 (Time 1) to complete our online survey. According to the market research company Bilendi & Respondi, we can expect a recall rate of about 60%, i.e., about n = 600. We will additionally recruit n = 1,050 for a total sample of n = 1,650 at Time 2.

In Study 2 (Time 3 - post-voting), we will invite all participants that completed Study 1 (Time 2- pre-voting). With a recall rate of about 60% (and excluding participants that failed our attention checks at Time 2), we expect to be able to recruit n = 891 at Time 3.
sample_size_rationale We used the software program G*Power to conduct a power analysis. Our goal was to obtain .80 power to detect a small effect size d = 0.20 at the standard .05 alpha error probability. Our power analysis shows that a sample of n = 788 is needed to have 80% power to detect a small effect size d = 0.20 for our independent t-tests (two-tailed). Given that we want participants at Time 3 to have completed the questionnaire at Time 2, and we can expect a recall rate of about 60%, a sample of at least n = 1,313 at Time 2 is needed in order to have about n = 788 participants at Time 3. As we have two attention checks in our survey at Time 2 (with an expected 10% failure rate in total), and another attention check at Time 3 (with an expected 10% failure rate), we aim to recruit n = 1,650 at Time 2. We expect to be able to resample about n = 600 participants from Time 1 at Time 2 and will invite an additional n = 1,050 to complete our survey at Time 2. All participants at Time 2 (pre-voting), will then be recontacted to fill out our survey at Time 3 (post-voting).

Recruitment overview:

Time 2: Resampled from Time 1 (at a 60% resampling rate) → n = 600
Time 2: Recruitment of additional sample of n = 1,050
Time 2: Final sample post attention check fails (assuming 10% failure rate) → n = 1,485

Time 3: Resampled from Time 2 (at a 60% resampling rate) → n = 891
Time 3: Final sample post attention check fails (assuming 10% failure rate) → n = 802
stopping_rule In T2, data collection will be stopped as soon as the target sample size of n = 1,485 has been reached. In T3, data collection will be stopped as soon as the target sample size of n = 788 has been reached.
manipulated_variables We manipulate the information that participants receive in the treatment versus control condition. In T2, participants in the control condition receive an explanatory text on popular initiatives, are informed that the climate protection law is an example of a counter-proposal to a popular initiative and that it enjoys large support among politicians, businesses, and associations. Participants in the treatment condition at T2 receive a text that includes original statements taken from a letter signed by over 230 scientists in support of the climate protection law. Participants in the treatment condition at T3 receive three sentences that state that scientists were either advocating for a law supported by the majority of the public or not, depending on the outcome of the voting. The control condition will not see any additional information.
measured_variables We will measure the following variables (see also questionnaires attached):

Climate change concern: 1 item, measured with a five-point scale (1 = not at all, 5 = very much)

Pluralistic ignorance: 3 items, Item 1 measured with a slider from 0-100%, Item 2 measured with a five-point scale (1 = not at all, 5 = very much), Item 3 measured with a five-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree)

Trust government: 1 item, measured with a five-point scale (1 = not at all, 5 = very much)

Social trust: Binary measure (0 = People can be trusted, 1 = You can’t be too careful when dealing with others)

Awareness of CPL: 1 item, measured with a five-point scale (1 = not at all, 5 = very familiar)

Representativeness of scientists: 1 item, measured with a five-point scale (1 = not at all, 5 = very strongly)

Objectivity of scientists: 1 item, measured with a five-point scale (1 = not at all, 5 = strongly strongly)

Voting intentions: Categorical measure (0 = Yes, 1 = No, 2 = I would abstain, 3 = I am not sure)

Acceptability of law: 1 item, measured with a five-point scale (1 = measures are too strong, 5 = measures are too weak, 99 = Don’t know)

Support for future climate protection laws: 1 item, measured with a five-point scale (1 = not at all, 5 = very much)

Trust in scientists: 12 items on 4 dimensions, measured with five-point scales (1 = very inexpert, very unintelligent, very unqualified, etc. to 5 = very expert, very intelligent, very qualified, etc.):
Competence
- How expert or inexpert are most scientists?
- How intelligent or unintelligent are most scientists?
- How qualified or unqualified are most scientists when it comes to conducting high-quality - research?
Integrity
- How honest or dishonest are most scientists?
- How ethical or unethical are most scientists?
- How sincere or insincere are most scientists?
Benevolence
- How concerned or not concerned are most scientists about people’s wellbeing?
- How eager or uneager are most scientists to improve others’ lives?
- How considerate or inconsiderate are most scientists of others’ interests?
Openness
- How open are most scientists to feedback?
- How willing or unwilling are most scientists to be transparent?
- How much or little attention do scientists pay to others’ views?

Normative perceptions of the role of science in society and politics: 5 items asking for the level agreement with five statements, measured with 5-point scales (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)
- Scientists should work closely with politicians to integrate scientific results into policy-making.
- Scientists should actively advocate for specific policies.
- Scientists should communicate their findings to politicians.
- Scientists should be more involved in the policy-making process.
- Scientists should communicate about science with the general public.

Participated in voting: Binary measure (0 = Yes, 1 = No)

Actual voting behavior: Categorical measure (0 = Yes, 1 = No, 2 = Prefer not to say)

Reasons for not voting: Categorical measure (0 = I wanted to abstain, 1 = I was unsure what to vote, 2 = I am not eligible to vote in Switzerland, 3 = Other (please describe))

Gender: Categorical measure (0 = female, 1 = male, 2 = prefer to self-describe, 99 = prefer not to say)

Age: Metric measure (in years)

Educational attainment: Categorical measure (0 = did not attend school, 1 = primary education, 2 = secondary education, 3 = higher education)

Region of origin: Categorical measure (0 = Switzerland, 1 = European Union/EFTA, 2 = Other (third states)

Canton of residence: List with all cantons

Language region: Categorical measure (0 = German, 1 = Italian, 2 = French, 3 = Romansh)

Voting eligibility: Categorical measure (0 = Yes, 1 = No, 2 = Don’t know)

Income: Metric measure (household’s yearly net income in local currency)

Urban/rural region of residence: Binary measure (1 = rural, 2 = urban)

Political orientation: 1 item asking respondents to self-classify as left-leaning or right-leaning, measured with a 5-point scale (1 = strongly left-leaning to 5 = strongly right-leaning)

Party preference: Categorical measure (0 = SVP, 1 = SP, 2 = FDP, 3 = GPS, 4 = GLP, 5 = The Centre, 6 = EVP, 7 = FDU, 8 = Ensemble à gauche, 9 = Lega dei Ticinesi, 10 = Other (please describe), 99 = I don’t know)

Religiosity: 1 item asking respondents to report the extent to which they consider themselves as religious, measured with a 5-point scale (1 = not religious at all to 5 = very strongly religious)

Parenthood: Binary measure (1 = Yes, 0 = No)

Gender of children: Categorical measure (0 = Boy, 1 = Girl, 2 = Both, I have more than one child, 99 = Prefer not to say)
indices We will use the following indices:
- Trust in scientists: Mean index of all 12 items measuring trust in scientists (see above)
- Normative perceptions of the role of science in society and politics: Mean index of all 5 items asking for normative perceptions (see above)

transformations We will apply the following transformations:
- Gender (measured with four categories: 0 = female, 1 = male, 2 = self-describe, 99 = prefer not to say) will be used as a binary variable (0 = female, 1 = male) through excluding all respondents who indicated 2 or 99.
- Educational attainment (measured with four categories: 0 = none, 1 = primary, 2 = secondary, 3 = tertiary) will be recoded to a binary variable (1 = tertiary, 0 = secondary or lower).
- For regression models with interactions, we will center all continuous predictors.
inference_criteria We will use the standard p <. 05 criteria for determining if the results are significantly different from those expected if the null hypothesis were correct. We will use 2-tailed tests and report exact p-values in the manuscript.
data_exclusion_criteria No checks will be performed to determine eligibility for inclusion besides verification that each respondent passed the relevant attention checks. Please note that respondents who failed the attention checks will have been automatically excluded from the survey, so they will not be contained in the final samples.
exploratory_analyses Additionally, we will analyze whether there are:
- Statistically significant differences in the levels of trust in scientists among participants at T1 and those in the control group at T2 (paired t-test).
- Statistically significant differences in trust in scientists between the treatment groups in T2 and T3
- Statistically significant differences in climate change concern between participants at T1, T2, and T3
- Statistically significant differences in pluralistic ignorance between participants in the T2 and T3

If more than 10% in our sample select response options other than “female” or “male” when asked to indicate their gender, we will additionally run exploratory analyses with gender coded as 0 = female, 1 = male, 2 = other.
